cards.explanation: The answer is all the sons of the king. The text says Absalom, David's son, invited all the sons of the king. That means every brother, Amnon included. A sheepshearing party with every one of the king's sons on the list, and I think that's a lot of mules to park.

The answer is False. The servants are invited too. Absalom says, “Will the king and his servants please come with me?” He asks for the king and his servants, not the king alone, so the idea that he asks the king to leave them at home is false.

The answer is that they would be a burden to Absalom. David says, “we should not all go, or we would be a burden to you.” I think he's thinking of the host, friends. Picture the bill for feeding a king and his whole household. I'd say no too, and I can't even afford the sprinkles.

The answer is Amnon. Absalom says, “If not… please let my brother Amnon go with us.” Amnon is David's oldest son (2 Samuel 3:2), and the text has already told us about what he did to Tamar. Absalom is asking for that one by name.
The answer is that David asks, “Why should he go with you?” I think that question just sits there in the air for a second. David doesn't say more about it, and Absalom keeps pressing.

The answer is until Amnon's heart is merry with wine. That's the heavy part of this passage. Absalom orders, “Watch Amnon until his heart is merry with wine…” The young men are waiting for that moment and for Absalom's signal. I think this is a hard one to read.

The answer is True. Absalom tells them, “Do not be afraid. Have I not commanded you? Be courageous and valiant!” That's an order to kill a king's son, and I think it's hard to read. He's pushing them to go through with it.
The answer is that each one flees on his mule. The text says, “…each one fled on his mule.” All the other sons of the king got up and left. Mules were what they rode, and they used them to flee.

The answer is that Absalom has struck down all the king's sons. David hears, “Absalom has struck down all the sons of the king; not one of them is left!” Notice the report says ALL of them, friends. We're about to find out it isn't true.

The answer is True. The text says, “Then the king stood up, tore his clothes, and lay down on the ground.” The report he heard was that Absalom had struck down all the sons of the king. I think this one hurts, and tearing his clothes shows how hard the news hits him.

The answer is that only Amnon is dead. Jonadab, the son of David's brother Shimeah, says it plainly: “…only Amnon is dead.” The first report said all the sons were gone. Jonadab corrects it with one name.

The answer is since the day Amnon violated Tamar. Jonadab says, “…Absalom has planned this since the day Amnon violated his sister Tamar.” That tells us when the planning began. Jonadab names that day as the starting point.

The answer is False. Jonadab says, “Look, the sons of the king have arrived! It is just as your servant said.” The watchman sees men coming, and Jonadab says they're the king's sons, not Absalom's young men. Then the text says the sons of the king came in, wailing loudly.

The answer is True. The text says, “And as he finished speaking, the sons of the king came in, wailing loudly.” Jonadab had just said it, and there they are, alive. Then the king and all his servants weep very bitterly too.
The answer is mourns. The text says, “But David mourned for his son every day.” Not one day, friends, every day. I think that's a father who is hurting.
The answer is three years. The text says, “After Absalom had fled and gone to Geshur, he stayed there three years.” That's a long time to be away from home. Geshur is where Talmai, its king, lived.

The answer is True. The text says, “And King David longed to go to Absalom, for he had been consoled over Amnon’s death.” The grief has eased, and now he longs for the son who ran. I think that's a father's heart at work.
